title: Unborn, beyond the elements
hookLine: ajoo hain, abhoo hain: never born, not made of earth or water (Jaap, chachari)

cards: Everything you've ever touched was made of something. The table: wood, which was a tree, which was soil and rain and light. Your coffee: water, beans, heat.
Your own body: about sixty percent water, plus minerals that were once in the ground, plus the air in your lungs right now. Even you had a birthday: a day, a place, a mother.
Everything has a when it began and a what it's made of. Jaap Sahib names something that has neither.

teach.b: The two-word lines keep coming. Ajoo hain. Abhoo hain.
Joon is a Punjabi word for a birth, a life-form, a body you're born into.
Ajoo, and its fuller form ajooni, means never born into any form. If that sounds familiar, it should.
It's in the Mool Mantar, Guru Nanak's words that open the Guru Granth Sahib, the lines many Sikhs learn first: ajooni saibhang, unborn, self-existent.
Guru Arjan set them at the head of the scripture when he compiled it in 1604, and here the Tenth Guru brings the idea back, nearly two centuries after Guru Nanak, in his own morning praise.
The first Guru and the tenth, saying the same thing in different meters. Then abhoo.

Bhoo is the earth, the stuff things are made of; abhoo, not made of earth. Sikh scripture often speaks of the body as made of five elements, earth, water, fire, air and space, borrowed for a while and given back.
The One, Jaap says, isn't made of any of them. Not a very large person, not a force inside the world like gravity, but something not built from the world's materials at all.

Sikh teaching holds firmly that the One is never born and never dies. On an ordinary day, that matters. Everything you can touch will change, wear out and return to the ground, your own hands included.
That can be frightening. Ajooni says that what you bow to is not on that list.
Not made of this, so it can't wear out.

how: Sikhs say ajooni saibhang every day in the Mool Mantar at the start of Japji, and hear the same idea again in Jaap's ajoo hain, abhoo hain.

o: born again and again in many bodies
born long ago, before the world began
never born into any body or form

games.q: unborn, beyond the elements — tap the pairs.

s: the word ajooni first appears in Jaap Sahib
it's in the Mool Mantar at the start of the Guru Granth Sahib: ajooni saibhang.
Sikh scripture speaks of the body as made of five elements
earth, water, fire, air and space, borrowed for a while.
abhoo describes the One as made of a very fine kind of earth
it means not made of earth at all, not built from the world's materials.

games.q: the Tenth Guru is writing his morning praise. which earlier Sikh words does he echo in ajoo hain?
o: a line from a Persian poem.
games.why: Guru Nanak's opening lines call the One ajooni, unborn; the Tenth Guru brings it back nearly two centuries later.

practice: Put your fingers on something solid, soil, a stone, the floor, then on something wet, a glass of water or a damp cloth: both made, and your hand is made of them too.
Now rest your hand in your lap and let your attention go past what you can touch, to the quiet behind it. If you pray, you can say ajooni softly.

wordCard.voice: Ajooni. Never born into any body: the word from the Mool Mantar that Jaap echoes with ajoo hain, abhoo hain, unborn and not made of earth.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: ajooni, never born into any body, from joon, a birth; in the Mool Mantar.

carryVoice: Your line: not made of this. Whatever wears out, the One you bow to doesn't. See you tomorrow.
